subject: UNITCHECK inside a string eval never runs (op/catch.t t2/t6) — needs a call on where an eval'd unit's compile boundary is
description:
DIAGNOSED s319, NOT fixed — the fix needs a semantics decision, see below.

  eval 'BEGIN { die } 123'      perl: undef   PCL: undef    CORRECT
  eval 'UNITCHECK { die } 123'  perl: undef   PCL: **123**  WRONG
  eval 'die; 123'               perl: undef   PCL: undef    CORRECT
  eval '123'                    perl: 123     PCL: 123      CORRECT

So only UNITCHECK diverges, and it is precisely isolated.

CAUSE (read, not guessed): UNITCHECK thunks are pushed onto *unitcheck-blocks*
and drained ONLY at the MAIN program's compile->run boundary
(p-run-compile-phase-blocks, cl/pcl-runtime.lisp:906).  Its docstring says
blocks registered later — "a runtime require or eval" — are perl's "too late to
run" case and never fire.  That is right for a runtime *require*, but WRONG for
a string eval: an eval'd string is its OWN compilation unit, and perl runs its
UNITCHECK at the end of compiling it (which is the entire point of UNITCHECK as
distinct from CHECK).

WHY I DID NOT JUST FIX IT.  The obvious patch — bind *unitcheck-blocks* to nil
around p-eval's form loop and drain it at the end, inside the existing
handler-case so a die lands in $@ — makes these two rows pass, but it runs
UNITCHECK **after** the eval'd code's runtime part, whereas perl runs it
**between** compile and run.  For `UNITCHECK { die } 123` both orders return
undef, so the test cannot tell them apart; for an eval whose runtime part has
side effects, they differ observably.  p-eval reads-and-evaluates form by form
(deliberately — so an in-package takes effect, see its comment), so there is no
clean compile/run split to hang the drain on.

THE QUESTION FOR FABLE/USER: where is an eval'd unit's compile boundary in
PCL's read-eval-per-form model, and is "drain at the end of the form loop" an
acceptable approximation (2 rows pass, ordering subtly wrong) or should the
eval seam gain a real two-phase split first?  Related: #91 established the
phase-block machinery; this is the one place its "too late" rule is too broad.

SCOREBOARD: op/catch.t is 10/2 vs perl 12/0; these two rows are the whole gap.
